paras: The Freetown killings took place on August 16, 1888, when an armed body of white men from three south Louisiana parishes besieged a house in Freetown, a Black settlement in Iberia Parish, and shot dead between ten and twenty Black men who had armed themselves there. One white attacker, the New Iberia civil engineer E. Payson Smith, was killed while forcing the door. The affair became a partisan issue: Southern papers called it a 'war of races', while Northern Republican papers and a senator called it murder.

The fight followed a campaign by 'regulators' in neighboring Vermilion Parish, where young men of Abbeville whipped people they considered bad characters with cowhides and were fired on at the house of a white woman living with a mulatto. According to the New Iberia dispatches, people driven out of Abbeville and St. Martinsville took refuge in Freetown, and Iberia's Black town officers had lately been forced by a citizens' committee to resign.

The Picayune's correspondent described Freetown as about fifteen Black families on four square miles. He wrote that Andy Smith, accused of stealing from white neighbors, had been told by regulators that he would be whipped, and gathered sixteen to eighteen armed men. The wire account instead spoke of hundreds of armed Black men gathering from August 12 to protect the refugees.

On Thursday afternoon, 150 to 500 whites rode into Freetown and demanded that the Black men give up their arms and disperse. Most did, but twelve to eighteen barricaded themselves in the new house of their pastor, given as Rev. Celeste Noop or H. Nora, and refused a twenty-minute ultimatum.

The white accounts say a volley came from the door before the time was up, and that firing went on for about an hour and a half. Smith then rushed the house with one companion and was shot as he forced the door. The Picayune estimated 400 to 500 shots and reported that several men who escaped were shot while running. A dispatch quoted by the Chicago Citizen added that a posse under Capt. C. T. Cole of the Atta Kapas Rangers found one wounded man feigning death, struck him with a rawhide, and shot him when he ran.

Bodies were left in the 'negro church' for the coroner, and the Picayune named the dead as Sam Cohil, Earnest Grient, Andy Smith, Paul Charles, Louis Simmons and Tom Simon, with four more names from a Black informant. The coroner's jury found ten Black men killed and a number wounded, among them the school teacher Alex Lee. Smith was buried at New Iberia with military and civic honors.

No arrests were reported. An Address issued in New Orleans in the name of the colored people of Louisiana called Freetown 'the latest wholesale murder' by a 'fraudulently installed' sheriff and his men, and predicted that no arrests would follow.

The first special, of August 16, said Smith had been killed 'by citizens' of Freetown for stirring up the negroes; later dispatches made him one of the attackers. Wire headlines such as 'A War of Races. Indignant Whites and Disreputable Blacks Clash' presented the whites' version, and weeklies in Monroe and St. Martinville reprinted the Picayune's account as 'full and fair' and 'about correct', the latter blaming Andy Smith's 'daredevil rascality'.

The Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted in Yankton under 'The Bloody Shirt', called the attackers assassins and said the Associated Press at New Orleans had not reported the affair. The Chicago Citizen predicted that no white man would be punished, and Senator Chandler told the Senate the Freetown men 'were peaceful' victims of Democratic intimidation. Weekly summaries gave the event one line, 'thirteen negroes' killed, and a South Carolina brief a month later said no white man had died.
The Address, printed in the Huntsville Gazette in September, is the only account in the coverage that gives the Black community's version.

Counts of the Black dead ran from seven to 'more than twenty'; the coroner's jury figure of ten was reported in the North as a correction of the twenty. That the besieged fired first rests on the whites' word, while the Address described a midnight attack by a sheriff's party without a warrant.

reader.title: Freetown killings (1888)
bases: An armed body of whites from three parishes, described as regulators, citizens or a posse, besieged armed Black men in a house in the Black settlement of Freetown and killed between ten and twenty of them (A13, A25, A26, A28).

Ten or more Black men were shot by a body of 150 to 500 whites acting, by their own accounts, to disarm and disperse 'idle and immoral' refugees and to punish Andy Smith; no account describes a warrant, and the Address says there was none (A13, A25, A32). Because the killings came in an armed exchange in which a white man was killed, the case is closer to a massacre in a siege than a classic lynching, though one wire account describes a wounded man who had feigned death being shot as he ran (A28).

Independent New Iberia wire dispatches, the Picayune's Lafayette correspondent, the coroner's jury report and the colored citizens' Address all agree that whites besieged armed Black men at Freetown and killed many of them (A8, A13, A14, A26, A32); only the late Abbeville Press and Banner brief denies Smith's death (A34).

accounts.label: New Iberia wire dispatch (whites' version)
accounts.gist: Armed negroes gathered at Freetown to protect refugees; after most surrendered their arms, a dozen or so in a minister's house refused a twenty-minute ultimatum and fired first; Smith was killed forcing the door and thirteen negroes died.

accounts.label: Picayune correspondent at Lafayette
accounts.gist: Andy Smith, accused of thefts and threatened with whipping, armed sixteen to eighteen men and defied the whites, who gathered 150 to 500 strong, parleyed, and then fought; the dead numbered ten to twenty.

accounts.label: Aug. 18 dispatch quoted by The Citizen
accounts.gist: A large posse under Capt. C. T. Cole poured fire into the house, killed occupants who tried to escape, and shot a wounded man who had been shamming death.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: On visiting the scene, the coroner and jury found ten negroes killed and a number wounded.

accounts.label: Address of the colored people of Louisiana
accounts.gist: A fraudulently installed sheriff and his men, with no warrant, invaded the village at midnight and slaughtered men who had gathered in a house for self-defence; no arrests would follow.

framing.detail: Wire headlines such as 'A War of Races. Indignant Whites and Disreputable Blacks Clash' and 'E. P. Smith, a Civil Engineer, Killed by Negroes' presented the whites' account as fact.
The St. Martinville Weekly Messenger called the Picayune account 'about correct' and blamed Andy Smith's 'daredevil rascality'; the Monroe Ouachita Telegraph called it 'a full and fair account'.
The Kennebec Journal's headline 'Banishing the Immoral. Is the Excuse Made for a Fight' signalled doubt about the stated motive.
The Chicago Inter-Ocean, reprinted as 'The Bloody Shirt', called the attackers assassins and said the Southern press and Associated Press played the affair down.
The Chicago Citizen's 'Negro Murdering in the South' said no white man would be punished and called on the federal government to act.
Sen. Chandler called the Freetown killings an atrocious murder aimed at keeping Louisiana solidly Democratic.
Weekly news summaries ran one line: the race war 'culminated on the 17th in the killing of thirteen negroes'.

conflicts.note: The coroner's jury count of ten is the only official figure; the Republican Journal reported it as a correction of the 'twenty'.
Every contemporary account names Smith as killed; the denial comes from a late, brief South Carolina summary.

Freetown, a Black settlement about ten miles from New Iberia, near Cade's station and Burk station on the Morgan road
